In January 2026 Fernwood Systems replaced our timestamp-based build cache with a content-addressed one.
The old cache keyed each artifact on the modification time of the files that produced it.
The new cache keys every artifact on the SHA-256 hash of its declared inputs.
Two builds with identical inputs are guaranteed to resolve to the same cache entry regardless of when they ran.
Median CI build time on our main branch fell from 14 minutes to 3 minutes 20 seconds after the migration.
The cache hit rate on that branch now sits at 82 percent, measured over the eight weeks since the cutover.
The migration took six weeks of one engineer's time.
The migration required rewriting 41 build files to declare their inputs explicitly.
Roughly a third of those files were reading configuration from the environment without declaring it.
Storage costs rose from $310 to $1,900 per month.
We retain evicted cache entries for 30 days so that a bisect across a release window still hits warm entries.
The hardest part was not the hashing. It was teaching the build to be honest about its inputs.
We evaluated moving to a remote execution cluster at the same time and decided against it for now.
The cache alone recovered most of the wall-clock win.
Remote execution would have added a second failure domain to every build.
We expect to revisit that decision once the cache hit rate stops improving.
The rollout to the other three engineering teams is planned for the third quarter of 2026.
The content-addressed cache is less about storage and more about honesty.

The three arrays generated 11,208 megawatt-hours in 2025.

Harbor, a payroll software company with 60 employees based in Manchester, has acquired Lantern, a note-taking app made by a twelve-person company in Leeds.
Neither company disclosed the price.

This spring we rewrote our billing service, which was originally written in Python, in Go.
The rewrite cut the service's p99 latency from 840 milliseconds to 95 milliseconds.
The rewrite reduced its memory use by about two thirds.
The rewrite took four engineers eleven weeks.

The Kestrel Fen Trust completed its ninth annual transect survey of Thornlee Marsh between 12 and 19 May 2026.
Eleven transects were walked, the same eleven as in every year since 2018.
We logged 214 breeding pairs of reed bunting across the eleven transects.
We recorded four occupied territories of marsh harrier with confidence.
We think there may be a fifth marsh harrier occupied territory on the northern edge.
That marsh harrier pair was never seen carrying food.
We are not counting that marsh harrier pair.
Water levels averaged 41 cm across the season.
The water levels are roughly a third below the ten-year mean.
The exact ten-year mean is being recomputed.
The 62 cm figure we published last year should be treated as provisional.

We have no photograph, no spraint from that stretch, and the Trust's camera trap was offline that week.
The sighting is unconfirmed.

We expect to publish the full survey report in September, assuming the logger data can be recovered.
Whether the Trust extends the survey to the adjoining Barrow Levels in 2027 has not been decided and depends on funding.

Every conference talk I have ever sat through celebrates the person who built the thing.
Nobody gives a keynote about the person who kept it running.
I spent four years, from 2019 to 2023, maintaining the shift-scheduling system at Bracken & Doyle.
The shift-scheduling system assigned shifts to about 9,000 warehouse workers across 23 sites.
In a normal week, the system processed roughly 30,000 shift assignments.
The system was written before I arrived and will outlive everyone who currently touches it.
My team — there were three of us — did not build it. We kept it honest.
In 2021 the company approved a full rewrite, budgeted at eighteen months.
The rewrite was cancelled after fourteen months, with roughly $2 million spent and nothing shipped to production.
The rewrite team was talented, and the plan was not absurd.
It failed for the boring reason most rewrites fail: the old system's real specification lived in a decade of accumulated fixes that no document recorded.

Over the same fourteen months, our three-person maintenance team shipped 41 releases, and the production incident count fell from 31 in the quarter the rewrite started to 6 in the quarter it was cancelled.
The unglamorous work was not merely cheaper. It was the only work that was actually improving the thing the business ran on.
Stewardship compounds and novelty mostly does not.
A maintainer who closes one confusing failure mode makes every future incident easier to diagnose; a greenfield team learns things the production system already knew.
I think the industry's rewards — promotion criteria, conference programs, the word 'impact' itself — are calibrated to the wrong one of these two curves.
I left Bracken & Doyle in 2023, and the scheduling system is still running.
I consider that the proudest line on my résumé, and I have stopped apologizing for it.
